beats.narration: Which model should I use? It's usually the first question developers ask, and Claude gives you a whole family to choose from. In the next three minutes you'll learn the four tiers, and a second lever that's just as important, and often confused with the first: reasoning.

The family spans four tiers. Haiku is built for speed and cost efficiency, when the task fits its capability envelope. Sonnet is the balanced default for most production work. Opus handles demanding work above the Sonnet envelope. And Fable is the most capable tier, built for the hardest reasoning, coding, and agentic work. Here's the practical rule: start with Sonnet. Move up a tier only when an eval shows the current tier missing your quality bar. And move down to Haiku only when an eval shows the quality drop is acceptable. Notice the pattern: evals make the call, not vibes. One more thing: the family evolves, so confirm the current lineup in the docs when you build.

↓ only when an eval says the drop is OK
lineup evolves: check docs at build time

beats.narration: Now the second lever. Whether the model reasons before answering is not a model choice. It's a separate setting you make on every call. On current models this is adaptive thinking: the model decides when and how much to think, and you tune the depth with an effort setting. Watch out if you've used this before: the old fixed token budget control is deprecated, and on the newest models it returns an error. Also, thinking content is hidden from responses by default now. If you need to show it, request the summarized display. So when does reasoning earn its cost? On hard, multi-step problems. On lookups and simple classification, it's wasted tokens.

beats.narration: Because the two levers are independent, they compose. A capable model with reasoning off is fast and direct. A smaller model with reasoning on spends extra tokens to think. And for the most demanding tasks, you pair a capable model with a higher effort setting. Module two teaches the mechanics of enabling reasoning, and module four takes up the full cost and quality decision.

elements.text: capable model + reasoning off  →  fast & direct
smaller model + reasoning on  →  pays tokens to think
capable model + high effort  →  the hardest work
M2: the mechanics · M4: cost vs quality

beats.narration: So remember: model choice picks the family member. Reasoning is configured per request. Start with Sonnet, let your evals move you up or down, and spend reasoning only where the problem is genuinely hard. Next up: prompting modes.

items.text: reasoning only for genuinely hard problems
